name: Sumer
description: The world's first urban civilization, in southern Mesopotamia: city-states like Uruk and Ur invented cuneiform writing, the sexagesimal system behind our minutes and degrees, monumental temple platforms (ziggurats), and the earliest known literature, including Gilgamesh.

name: Ancient Egypt
description: The Nile civilization of pharaohs, hieroglyphs, and pyramid-building, remarkable for three millennia of institutional continuity — divine kingship, mortuary religion, and a scribal bureaucracy sustained by the river's annual flood.

name: Indus Valley Civilization
description: South Asia's first urban culture — Harappa and Mohenjo-daro featured grid streets, standardized bricks and weights, and sophisticated drainage — yet left an undeciphered script and little evidence of kings or armies.

name: Ancient Greece
description: A civilization of competitive city-states that produced democracy in Athens, philosophy from Socrates to Aristotle, tragedy and history as genres, the Olympic games, and — via Alexander — a Hellenistic koine spanning three continents.

name: Roman Empire
description: The Mediterranean superstate whose legions, roads, aqueducts, cities, law, and Latin language framed European civilization; its citizenship model, engineering, and legal code remain foundational.

name: Maya Civilization
description: Mesoamerican civilization of the Yucatán and highlands: the Americas' only fully developed pre-Columbian writing system, positional mathematics with zero, precise astronomical calendars, and dynastic city-states like Tikal and Calakmul.

name: Han China
description: The dynasty that fixed China's imperial template: Confucian civil service, census bureaucracy, the Silk Road opened to the west, and inventions including paper. 'Han' remains the name of China's majority people.

name: Byzantine Empire
description: The Greek-speaking continuation of Rome centred on Constantinople: Orthodox Christianity, Justinian's law code, iconography, and a fortress-economy that shielded Europe's southeastern flank for a millennium.

name: Abbasid Caliphate
description: The Islamic empire at its cultural height, ruling from purpose-built Baghdad: translation of the world's science into Arabic, algebra and optics, paper-making learned from Chinese prisoners, and a cosmopolitan mercantile world from al-Andalus to the Indies.

name: Norse Vikings
description: Scandinavian seafarers whose longships raided monasteries, founded Dublin, Normandy, and the Kievan Rus trade route, settled Iceland and Greenland, and reached Newfoundland five centuries before Columbus.

name: Mongol Empire
description: The largest contiguous land empire in history, from Korea to Hungary: devastating in conquest, then guarantor of the Pax Mongolica under which merchants, missionaries, technologies — and eventually the plague — moved freely across Eurasia.

name: Inca Empire
description: The Andes' great empire, run without writing or wheels: khipu cord-records, 40,000 km of mountain roads with relay runners, terraced agriculture, freeze-dried storehouses, and monumental masonry at Cusco and Machu Picchu.

name: Aztec Empire
description: The Triple Alliance dominating central Mexico from the island capital Tenochtitlan — a city of canals and chinampa gardens larger than contemporary European capitals — with tribute economics, pictographic books, and a calendar-driven sacrificial religion.

name: Ottoman Empire
description: The Turkish empire that took Constantinople, ruled the Balkans, Anatolia, and the Arab lands for centuries, and governed its diverse subjects through the millet system — a great power of gunpowder, bureaucracy, and monumental mosque architecture into the twentieth century.

name: Edo Japan
description: Two and a half centuries of enforced peace under the Tokugawa shoguns: samurai turned administrators, foreign contact restricted to Nagasaki, and a flourishing urban culture of kabuki, haiku, and woodblock prints in million-strong Edo.
